title: Gas, Fees, and Rent on Solana
objectives: Why every transaction carries a fee, and how Solana prices it
What rent is, and why closing an empty account gives you SOL back
The path a transaction takes from your click to final

steps.title: The fee is a postage stamp
steps.body:
Every <Term id="transaction">transaction</Term> carries a small <Term id="gas_fee">fee</Term>, paid in SOL. A postage stamp is the right mental model: your message doesn't travel for free, but it travels cheap.

The base fee on Solana is 5,000 lamports per signature. That's 0.000005 SOL, a fraction of a cent. Read the unit carefully, though - *per signature*. A plain transfer has one signer and costs one stamp. A transaction with three signers pays for three.

The fee does two jobs. It pays the validators running the network, and it makes spam expensive - if a transaction were free, anyone could flood the network with garbage at no cost.

The part that surprises people coming from Ethereum: the base fee is flat. It doesn't bid up with congestion. What rises when the network gets busy is the optional priority fee, which is a Pro-tier topic. The base fee stays at 5,000 lamports no matter how loud the chain gets.

steps.title: What rent actually is
steps.body:
On Solana, data lives in accounts, and an account costs the network memory forever. So the network asks for a deposit up front: enough SOL to make the account *rent-exempt*. For a token account, that works out to about 0.00203928 SOL.

Two things follow, and both catch people out.

- You never pay it over time. Rent collection was switched off. The requirement is simply that an account is funded above the exempt threshold when it's created. Fund it and it stays on-chain indefinitely.
- Closing the account returns the whole deposit to your wallet. You are not paying the network for storage. You are parking collateral against it, and getting it back when you leave.

That's why cleaning up empty accounts is a real habit rather than a ritual. Each one you close returns about 0.002 SOL. It's also why creating a brand-new token account costs a little: somebody is funding that deposit, and for the first time you receive a token, it's usually the sender who pays it.

steps.title: From click to final
steps.body:
A signed transaction is a small package: a list of instructions, every account address those instructions will touch, a recent blockhash, and your <Term id="signature">signature</Term>.

The blockhash is there to stop replays. It expires after about 150 blocks - roughly a minute - so a transaction can't be captured and resubmitted later by someone else. If you've ever seen a transaction fail with an expired blockhash, this is why.

From there your RPC provider forwards it to the current leader, the validator whose turn it is to produce a block. Solana executes transactions in parallel through a runtime called Sealevel, using the account list to know which transactions can't touch the same data at once. A slot lasts about 400 milliseconds.

You'll see three words for the outcome. *Processed* means a validator ran it. *Confirmed* means a supermajority of stake has voted on it. *Finalized* means it's rooted and cannot be reverted. For anything you care about, wait for finalized - it arrives a few seconds after you sign.

questions.prompt: What currency is used to pay the base transaction fee on Solana?
options: SOL, the native token of Solana
questions.explainRight: SOL. Every base fee on Solana is denominated in it.
questions.explainWrong: SOL. The native token is the only thing the network accepts for fees.

questions.prompt: What happens to the rent deposit when you close an empty token account?
options: It is refunded to your wallet
questions.explainRight: You get it back. Rent is a refundable deposit, not a payment - closing the account returns the SOL.
questions.explainWrong: It comes back. The deposit returns to your wallet when the account closes.
